what: StepStone Group advises institutions on private markets. It helps pension funds, sovereign wealth funds and insurers decide where to commit money across private equity, private credit, infrastructure and real estate, manages funds on their behalf, and sells the data underpinning those decisions.
customers: Public and corporate pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, insurers and endowments, and increasingly wealthy individuals accessing private markets through intermediaries.
money: Fees on assets under management and advisement across private market strategies.
A share of gains once thresholds are met, plus returns on the firm’s own investments.
moat: Private markets are opaque, and StepStone holds decades of fund-level performance data that nobody can assemble retrospectively. That data makes its advice credible, which attracts commitments, which generate more data. Institutional clients also commit for a decade or more, so the relationship and the fee base are unusually long-lived.
risks: A trailing net loss of $318.3M and free cash flow of about negative $817.6M — the accounting consolidates funds the firm manages, which makes the reported figures very hard to read.
Revenue history is erratic, showing $1.4B in 2022, negative $67.6M in 2023 and $2.0B in 2026, reflecting investment gains and losses rather than fee income.
Private markets fundraising has slowed considerably, which directly affects the commitments StepStone’s revenue depends on.
Ten analysts average a $65.60 target against a $43.84 price, a 50% gap reflecting disagreement about the fundraising cycle.
A sustained period of poor private equity returns would damage both the fee base and the premise of advising on the asset class.
opportunities: Fee-paying assets are committed for a decade or more, which makes the underlying fee revenue unusually predictable once the reported noise is stripped out.
Cash of $1.1B against $378.6M of debt is a strong position.
Access to private markets for wealthy individuals rather than only institutions is a large new channel where StepStone is well positioned.
Decades of fund-level performance data is an asset competitors cannot replicate.
Revenue has grown substantially over the period, from $1.4B in 2022 to $2.0B in 2026.
watch: Fee-earning assets under management and new commitments. The reported income statement is dominated by consolidation and investment marks; the fee base is the business.
view: The first thing to do with StepStone is separate the business from the accounting, because the reported figures are close to unreadable. A trailing net loss of $318 million, negative free cash flow of $818 million, and a revenue line that showed negative $67.6 million in one year and $2.0 billion in another — none of that describes an advisory firm. It describes consolidation of the funds the firm manages, plus mark-to-market movements on its own investments. The business underneath is fee-earning assets under management and the fees charged on them.

That business is a good one. StepStone gets paid for helping institutions decide where to commit capital in private markets and for managing the resulting programmes. It does not need to generate investment returns itself to earn its fee, the capital is committed for a decade or more, and the underlying data asset — decades of fund-level performance information — makes the advice credible in a market where information is genuinely scarce. The loop is self-reinforcing: data brings credibility, credibility brings commitments, commitments generate data.

The cyclical problem is real and currently biting. Private markets fundraising has slowed sharply: institutions are over-allocated to private equity, exits are slow, and the distributions that would fund new commitments are not arriving. Since StepStone’s revenue follows commitments, that flows straight through. The individual-investor channel — opening private markets to wealthy individuals rather than only institutions — is the structural offset, and StepStone is well positioned in it.

What would turn a cyclical slowdown into a structural one is sustained poor private equity returns, because that would weaken both the fee base and the premise of advising on the asset class at all. The ten analysts at $65.60 against $43.84 are betting on the cycle. I would want to see fee-earning assets and new commitments, which lead revenue by about a year, and I would ignore the income statement entirely.
bull: Private markets fundraising recovers as exits clear, the individual-investor channel opens a large new source of commitments, and an irreplaceable data asset compounds.
bear: Institutions stay over-allocated, private equity returns disappoint for years, and consolidated accounting hides deterioration in the underlying fee base.
